source.title: Data Scaling Laws in NMT: The Effect of Noise and Architecture
source.authors: Yamini Bansal; B. Ghorbani; Ankush Garg; Biao Zhang; M. Krikun; Colin Cherry; Behnam Neyshabur; O. Firat

record.tranche_reason: Extends data-scaling-law tests to supervised neural machine translation and varies architecture, data quality, and noise.
record.gate_note: The paper tests held-out NMT test loss as training data increases, not language-model pretraining loss as parameter count, tokens, or compute increase. It also reports BLEU scaling and comparisons of architecture and data conditions. Cited results from other papers are not recorded as rows.
record.test_reason: Fits held-out test loss against training-set size for supervised English-German NMT over about 3 orders of magnitude (1M-512M pairs). It varies shape, architecture, data source, filtering, noise, back-translation and dropout. This is a new training regime with its own results on V5, V6 and V7. V1-V4 concern LM pretraining, compute and fixed-parameter shape, which the study does not test.
record.authors_conclusion: Mostly right. The authors conclude that architecture, filtering, data-source and independent-noise changes mainly shift the scaling curve and barely change the exponent, so marginally worse setups can often be offset with more data. Two qualifications: independent source or target noise converges to a worse limiting loss, so more data cannot always compensate. Back-translated data has a lower exponent (~0.19 vs ~0.28) and a worse limiting loss.
record.recipe_differences: The study measures supervised NMT test loss against training dataset size and varies architectures and data conditions; it does not reproduce language-model pretraining scaling against parameters, tokens, and compute.
record.method_sensitivity: The fitted exponent changes between parallel and back-translated data and changes under Pareto dropout tuning; the paper reports different α and C across architectures and data conditions.

fits_no_version.finding: Loss differences between NMT architectures and data conditions sit in the multiplicative constant and capacity term, not the exponent. Worse setups can therefore be offset by a constant factor of more data.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Data-scaling exponents are invariant to architecture and data-quality changes, which act only as constant-factor data penalties.

record.problems: Evidence concerns NMT data scaling rather than language-model pretraining. The authors qualify generality for very different architectures or noise. Many curve values are presented in figures rather than tabulated; the text reports training-loss variation up to 2% from randomness and says larger-data variance is expected to be lower.
record.rows_left_out: Individual plotted outcomes for the 14 OOD test sets are not entered separately because their individual values and names are not stated in the supplied text; their aggregate textual result is recorded in R8.

untested.parts: LM pretraining loss versus parameters, tokens or compute. Only NMT data scaling is tested.
Extrapolation from small runs to runs orders of magnitude larger. R2 holds out a model shape, not a scale range.
Compute-optimal allocation between parameters and data.
Loss at fixed parameter count across depth and width. The shapes compared differ in parameter count, and the architecture comparison changes the model class.
Image or video models, repeated data, fine-tuning and transfer. Parameter scaling is not fitted here; it is borrowed from Ghorbani et al.
Downstream tasks other than the translation task's own BLEU.
Parameter-counting choices, training schedule and fitting method. Cross-paper disagreement is mentioned only via cited exponents.

missing.what: Fitting only dataset sizes ≥32M gives a loss exponent near 1 (O(1/D)): the curve bends from p ≈ 0.28 toward a variance-limited regime, with a later transition for larger models. This bears on curves bending away from a single power law.
missing.locator: Section 3 (Form of the Scaling Law); Appendix A.3, Figure 6; Appendix D

missing.what: Monte Carlo on 28L6L: a 2% loss SD from training randomness yields an exponent SD of 0.02. Separate per-model fits show minor exponent differences.
Chinese-English replication: the transformer and the LSTM hybrid share p = 0.25, and the OOD test sets share an exponent of 0.259.

record.verdict_notes: Common exponents were imposed in the joint fits, so 'exponent unchanged' rests on the authors' statement that the fits are good. The authors note their NMT data exponents (0.25-0.3) are much higher than Kaplan's LM data exponent. That comparison is cited, not a result of this study. The parameter-scaling terms in the joint law are borrowed from Ghorbani et al. (2021).

versions.untested_parts: The study is about supervised NMT, not language-model pretraining, and does not test loss scaling in parameters or compute.
It predicts an unseen model using a fit over the other data-model combinations, but does not fit on small runs and predict runs orders of magnitude larger.
No fixed-compute-budget allocation between parameter count and training tokens is tested.
The study compares selected NMT architectures and shapes; it does not systematically vary all architecture details or establish that loss differences are small across a wide range.
Tests supervised NMT data scaling, including architecture and data changes. Does not test image or video, repeated data, fine-tuning, or transfer.
Reports BLEU and its relationship with test log-perplexity for machine translation; does not test a broad set of downstream tasks or language-model pretraining loss.

Tests effects of data source, back-translation, and dropout fitting choices on NMT data-scaling exponents. Does not test parameter-counting choices, training schedules generally, or whether published language-model laws disagree.

rows.subject: encoder-decoder transformer models (2L6L, 6L2L, 6L6L, 6L28L, 28L6L)
rows.operation_detail: Fit held-out test log-perplexity against training dataset size.
rows.measure: test log-perplexity data-scaling exponent
rows.value: In the data-limited regime, loss scales as O(D^-1/4); the paper reports coverage of 3 orders of magnitude of training examples.
rows.note: The authors report that the same α and p fit all five shapes, with model-dependent C. This is NMT data scaling, not language-model pretraining.
rows.check: Correct as NMT data scaling. The law is the saturating form α(1/D+C)^p, not a pure power law.

rows.subject: joint data and parameter scaling law
rows.operation_detail: Fit α and p excluding all data-model combinations using a 6L2L model, then predict that model's test loss.
rows.measure: agreement of predicted and empirical test loss
rows.value: The joint law is described as accurately predicting out-of-sample test performance.
rows.locator: Section 3, Joint Data & Parameter Scaling Law; Figure 2A
rows.note: The fit excludes a model shape, not the larger end of a scale range.
rows.check: The held-out unit is a model shape (6L2L), not a larger scale, so this is not V2 evidence. The value is qualitative and read from Figure 2A only.

rows.subject: encoder-decoder transformer (2L6L, 6L2L, 6L6L, 6L28L, 28L6L)
rows.operation_detail: Compare data-scaling fits across encoder-decoder depth and shape configurations.
rows.measure: data-scaling fit parameters
rows.value: Common α and p are reported as sufficient across the five models; C changes with model capacity.
rows.locator: Section 3, Form of the Scaling Law; Figure 1A
rows.note: Shape-specific coefficients are not individually given in the text.
rows.check: Not V4: the five shapes differ in parameter count (170M-800M), and the measure is the shared data-scaling exponent, not loss at fixed N. For V5 the power-law form fits all five shapes. For V7 the exponent is invariant to shape, so the V7 effect is absent. The state field shows V5; for V7 it is absent.

source_check.correct: V5: observed. V7: absent for substantial shape-dependent exponent changes; common α and p fit the models, while separate fits show only minor exponent differences.
source_check.locator_found: Section 3, Form of the Scaling Law; Figure 1A; Appendix A.1.
source_check.problem: One observed state cannot describe both the power-law fit and the reported near-invariance of its exponent.

statements.correction: Section 3.2 and Appendix C: English-to-German data-scaling exponents are similar across source-original and target-original OOD test sets; news tests include WMT2019 newstest2019. No sentence-length-subset parameter-scaling experiment is reported. Architecture, filtering and independent-noise comparisons use shared fitted data exponents. Figure 5: fixed-dropout versus Pareto exponents are 0.267 versus 0.228 for English-to-German and 0.250 versus 0.201 for Chinese-to-English; authors characterize the changes as minor or the exponents as very similar.
statements.problem: The parameter-exponent, sentence-length-subset and WMT14 English-French claims are not results of this study. The shared-fit description and dropout exponents are correct.
